#### [Robust Equilibria in Cheap-Talk Games with Fairly Transparent Motives](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.04193)

::: {.news-copy .news-coauthors}
My paper with [Jan-Henrik Steg](https://pub.uni-bielefeld.de/person/182054), [Michael Greinecker](https://www.michaelgreinecker.com/), and [Christoph Kuzmics](https://sites.google.com/view/christoph-kuzmics) has received a revise-and-resubmit decision from *Games and Economic Behavior*.
:::

<details class="news-abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<p>For cheap-talk games with a binary state space in which the sender has state-independent preferences, we characterize equilibria that are robust to introducing slight state-dependence on the side of the sender. Not all equilibria are robust, but the sender-optimum is always achieved at some robust equilibrium.</p>
</details>
:::

#### [Multi-sender cheap talk with almost common information](https://ideas.repec.org/p/grz/wpaper/2026-22.html)

::: {.news-copy}
My job market paper is now online.
:::

<details class="news-abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<p>Multiple experts often observe information that is nearly, but not exactly, common. We study a multi-sender cheap talk model with an ε-mixture prior that varies correlation while holding marginals fixed. Correlation determines which message profiles are governed by Bayes' rule. Full revelation can be supported at perfect correlation, but any independent component rules it out. This is not a collapse of communication. Informative equilibria still exist with almost common information and can be partitional or nonpartitional. With similar information, partitional equilibria survive only on a strict subset of their perfect-correlation bias region, while nonpartitional equilibria remain feasible throughout their perfect-correlation bias region.</p>
</details>
:::

#### [Strategic Communication with Partial Expertise](https://ideas.repec.org/p/grz/wpaper/2026-23.html)

::: {.news-copy}
My new paper is now online.
:::

<details class="news-abstract">
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<p>Decision makers rely on experts who observe part of the information relevant to a choice. We study communication when an expert observes one component of a decision target but her observation also predicts a missing component. This indirect information can sustain communication despite conflicts of interest. The largest conflict consistent with informative communication depends on what extreme observations imply about the missing component, not on correlation alone. When this prediction is linear, higher correlation permits finer communication and raises the value of listening relative to no information. Yet this need not improve welfare because the decision itself becomes more difficult.</p>
</details>
:::
